PM2A-DIS-EB-012.q: A credible disinflation announcement lowers expectations before demand falls; contracts can reset immediately. Compare this with identical demand restraint under fixed old expectations.
options: Earlier contract adjustment increases the initial unemployment excursion by shifting SRPC upward.
Earlier contract adjustment leaves the excursion unchanged because expectations do not affect wages.
Earlier contract adjustment permanently lowers natural unemployment despite unchanged labor-market structure.
Earlier contract adjustment can reduce the initial unemployment excursion for that restraint.
PM2A-DIS-EB-012.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Earlier adjustment must raise the unemployment excursion because lower expected inflation shifts SRPC up” in this disinflation and policy task.
PM2A-DIS-EB-012.feedback: Lower expectations shift SRPC down before the contraction moves the economy along it. This can reduce the short-run output/employment cost, but is conditional on the explicitly rapid contract adjustment.

PM2A-DIS-EB-013.q: After disinflation, unemployment returns to its original natural rate and the inflation rate stabilizes at 2%. The price index is now 180, compared with 160 before. Which claim is supported?
options: Unemployment costs persist; the higher price level establishes continuing excess unemployment.
Unemployment costs have unwound; inflation of 2% makes the price index fall.
Unemployment costs have unwound; the price level remains higher and is still rising.
Unemployment costs cannot unwind; returning to natural requires the old price level.
PM2A-DIS-EB-013.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A higher price index proves disinflation failed regardless of the lower inflation rate” in this disinflation and policy task.
PM2A-DIS-EB-013.feedback: A successful reduction in positive inflation need not undo earlier price increases. Longer-run labor adjustment and the cumulative price-level path are different outcomes.

PM2A-DIS-L-010.q: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to natural. Which synthesis is correct?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
PM2A-DIS-L-010.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-DIS-L-010.feedback: The sacrifice ratio is 6/3=2 percent of annual output per percentage-point inflation reduction. The given return to natural unemployment means the unemployment cost is temporary in this model; disinflation alone need not make the price level fall.

PM2A-DIS-LB-018.q: After disinflation, unemployment returns to its original natural rate and the inflation rate stabilizes at 2%. The price index is now 260, compared with 240 before. Which claim is supported?
options: Unemployment costs persist; the higher price level establishes continuing excess unemployment.
Unemployment costs have unwound; inflation of 2% makes the price index fall.
Unemployment costs have unwound; the price level remains higher and is still rising.
Unemployment costs cannot unwind; returning to natural requires the old price level.
PM2A-DIS-LB-018.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A higher price index proves disinflation failed regardless of the lower inflation rate” in this disinflation and policy task.
PM2A-DIS-LB-018.feedback: A successful reduction in positive inflation need not undo earlier price increases. Longer-run labor adjustment and the cumulative price-level path are different outcomes.

PM2A-DIS-LB-019.q: Two disinflation plans reach the same inflation target. One has faster expectation adjustment and less cumulative excess unemployment. Does reaching the same target imply the same real transition cost?
options: Yes; any positive final inflation rate rules out real disinflation costs.
No; the path of excess unemployment can differ even with an identical final inflation rate.
Yes; final inflation alone determines all unemployment experienced during the transition.
No; lower excess unemployment proves the final natural unemployment rate changed.
PM2A-DIS-LB-019.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; final inflation alone determines all unemployment experienced during the transition.
PM2A-DIS-LB-019.feedback: An endpoint does not describe the transition path. Faster expectation adjustment can reduce excess unemployment incurred on the way to the same inflation target without requiring a different natural unemployment rate.

PM2A-DIS-LB-020.q: Inflation is down to 1% after disinflation, unemployment is back at natural, and the price level is higher than before. Which diagnosis is complete?
options: The price level should have returned to its starting value once unemployment normalized
Disinflation succeeded without requiring deflation; the short-run labor cost has unwound
Deflation occurred because the inflation rate fell even though prices remained higher
The natural rate must now be permanently lower because unemployment first increased
PM2A-DIS-LB-020.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
PM2A-DIS-LB-020.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

PM2A-SAC-EB-018.q: Use the sum of annual output-gap losses, measured as percentages of one year's output $180. Gaps are −2%, −1%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. An analyst divides by final inflation. Which correction is right?
options: The ratio is 4/7; divide by the initial inflation rate
The ratio is 1/2=0.5; only the final year's loss matters
The ratio is 4/2=2; divide cumulative loss by the two-point inflation reduction
The ratio is 4/5=0.8; divide by the final inflation rate
PM2A-SAC-EB-018.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The ratio is 4/7; divide by the initial inflation rate” in this sacrifice ratio task.
PM2A-SAC-EB-018.feedback: Cumulative loss is 2+1+1=4% of one year's output. The denominator is 7−5=2 percentage points, so the sacrifice ratio is 2, not loss divided by either inflation level.

PM2A-SAC-LB-023.q: Use the sum of annual output-gap losses, measured as percentages of one year's output $260. Gaps are −2%, −1%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. An analyst divides by final inflation. Which correction is right?
options: The ratio is 4/5=0.8; divide by the final inflation rate
The ratio is 4/7; divide by the initial inflation rate
The ratio is 1/2=0.5; only the final year's loss matters
The ratio is 4/2=2; divide cumulative loss by the two-point inflation reduction
PM2A-SAC-LB-023.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The ratio is 4/5=0.8; divide by the final inflation rate” in this sacrifice ratio task.
PM2A-SAC-LB-023.feedback: Cumulative loss is 2+1+1=4% of one year's output. The denominator is 7−5=2 percentage points, so the sacrifice ratio is 2, not loss divided by either inflation level.

PM2A-SAC-LB-024.q: A3-point disinflation was planned at sacrifice ratio 2, exhausting a 6% loss budget. The first point unexpectedly costs 4%. If remaining disinflation costs 2% per point, which claim about the original target and budget survives?
options: No further point can be achieved because the first loss exceeded its forecast
The target can increase because a larger first loss lowers all later losses mechanically
Only one further point fits the remaining 2% budget; achieving all 3 points would require total loss 8%
All remaining 2 points fit because the original average ratio remains 2 by assumption
PM2A-SAC-LB-024.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “No further point can be achieved because the first loss exceeded its forecast” in this sacrifice ratio task.
PM2A-SAC-LB-024.feedback: The unspent budget is 6−4=2. At 2% per point it buys one further point. Finishing the remaining two would cost 4 more and total 8; the original joint promises are no longer compatible.

PM2B1-GDPC-LB-001.q: Households buy $3 million of domestic services and $2 million of imports; firms buy $4 million of domestic machinery and $2 million of stock; government buys $5 million of domestic bridges and sends $1 million in transfers; exporters sell $2 million abroad. What is GDP from these transactions?
options: $14 million
$19 million
$17 million
$12 million
PM2B1-GDPC-LB-001.commonError: Adds financial transfers, used goods, or imported production to domestic GDP.
PM2B1-GDPC-LB-001.feedback: Domestic services add $3 million, domestic machinery adds $4 million, bridges add $5 million, and exports add $2 million. Imports, stock purchases, and transfers add no domestic production directly, so GDP is $14 million.

PM2B1-GDPC-MB-002.q: A domestic firm sells $100 of last year's inventory to households and produces $24 of new goods that remain unsold. No other production occurs. Which C, inventory-I and GDP entries are consistent?
options: C = $100, inventory I = $-76, GDP = $24
C = $100, inventory I = $24, GDP = $124
C = $0, inventory I = $-76, GDP = $-76
C = $100, inventory I = $76, GDP = $176
PM2B1-GDPC-MB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “C = $100, inventory I = $24, GDP = $124” in this gdp components task.
PM2B1-GDPC-MB-002.feedback: Consumption records the sale, but inventory investment is new accumulation 24 minus withdrawal 100. C+I = 100+(24−100) = $24, this year's production.

PM2B1-RNGDP-LB-001.q: The base-year economy produces 160 books at $4 and 80 meals at $10. Current quantities of both goods are 10% higher, but each current price is 20% higher. Which assessment of a reported 32% real-GDP growth rate is correct?
options: Nominal growth is 32%; real growth is 12% by simple subtraction.
Nominal growth is 32%; real growth is 10% at fixed prices.
Nominal growth is 32%; real growth is 20% from current prices.
Nominal growth is 32%; real growth is 32% including price changes.
PM2B1-RNGDP-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Real growth is 20%; the change in the price vector determines real output” in this real versus nominal gdp task.
PM2B1-RNGDP-LB-001.feedback: Quantities rise 10%, so valuation at unchanged base prices gives 10% real growth. Nominal growth compounds quantity and price factors: 1.10×1.20−1 = 32%. Exact deflation recovers 1.32/1.20−1 = 10%.

PM2B2-BIAS-FB-005.q: A product originally costs $230. Its replacement costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality changes. What should a quality-aware comparison avoid?
options: Treating the replacement as a new product; all quality gains must enter quantity only in every index
Holding service quality constant; comparable-price measurement should ignore quality
Calling the entire sticker-price increase inflation; cost per unit of service actually falls
Calling any of the sticker-price increase inflation; the price level of all other goods must fall
PM2B2-BIAS-FB-005.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Treating the replacement as a new product; all quality gains must enter quantity only in every index” in this cpi bias task.
PM2B2-BIAS-FB-005.feedback: The replacement's price per service unit is 1.20/2 = 0.60 of the old level. A like-for-like comparison must adjust for quality rather than automatically calling the full 20% higher price inflation.

PM2B2-BIAS-MB-001.q: A $250 payment is indexed to measured CPI. A careful study estimates measured inflation at 5% but the cost of maintaining the recipient's utility at 3%, owing to substitution and new choices. Which real-outcome comparison follows under these estimates?
options: Real value falls about 2%; measured inflation exceeds estimated cost growth.
Real value rises about 8%; add measured and estimated inflation rates.
Real value is unchanged; official indexation exactly preserves the recipient's utility.
Real value rises about 1.9%; indexation exceeds estimated cost growth.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The payment exactly preserves utility because any official index equals every household's cost of living” in this cpi bias task.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-001.feedback: The relevant factor is 1.05/1.03, about a 1.94% gain relative to the estimated utility-maintaining cost. The conclusion is conditional on the supplied estimates, not an assertion that every index overstates inflation by two points.

PM2B2-BIAS-MB-003.q: A product originally costs $270. Its replacement costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality changes. What should a quality-aware comparison avoid?
options: Holding service quality constant; comparable-price measurement should ignore quality
Calling the entire sticker-price increase inflation; cost per unit of service actually falls
Calling any of the sticker-price increase inflation; the price level of all other goods must fall
Treating the replacement as a new product; all quality gains must enter quantity only in every index
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Holding service quality constant; comparable-price measurement should ignore quality” in this cpi bias task.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-003.feedback: The replacement's price per service unit is 1.20/2 = 0.60 of the old level. A like-for-like comparison must adjust for quality rather than automatically calling the full 20% higher price inflation.

PM2B2-DEF-FB-005.q: A domestic economy buys $180 of imported household fuel and produces machinery only for export. Fuel prices rise while machinery prices are unchanged. Which index selection and direction are appropriate, holding quantities fixed?
options: Both rise equally; household fuel belongs in both indexes at equal weight.
CPI is unchanged; the GDP deflator rises through the import-price component.
CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
Both are unchanged; imported consumption is excluded from either price index.
PM2B2-DEF-FB-005.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Only the GDP deflator rises because imported fuel is subtracted through net exports” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
PM2B2-DEF-FB-005.feedback: CPI covers household consumption including imports. The GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output, including exports; unchanged domestic output prices need not reflect imported fuel inflation.

PM2B2-DEF-FB-006.q: A household benefit of $190 must track consumption costs, while an analyst must convert nominal domestic GDP into real output. Imported food becomes dearer and domestic investment equipment becomes cheaper. Which pairing and implication are supported?
options: CPI for both uses; consumer prices also measure domestic capital-goods prices.
CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
Deflator for both uses; domestic output prices measure imported household costs.
Deflator for benefits, CPI for GDP; imported food belongs to domestic output.
PM2B2-DEF-FB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Use the GDP deflator for both; household consumption excludes imported food” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
PM2B2-DEF-FB-006.feedback: The purpose determines index choice. CPI tracks consumption costs; the deflator matches domestic final output. Imports and investment equipment enter these measures differently, so divergent movements are possible.

PM2B2-DEF-L-002.q: A household grant rises from $2,000 to $2,160 as CPI moves from 125 to 135. Nominal GDP rises 8% while the GDP deflator rises 4%. Which combined assessment uses the appropriate indexes?
options: The grant gains 8% purchasing power; real GDP rises 8%
The grant loses purchasing power; real GDP is unchanged
Both real changes are zero because each nominal value rose 8%
The grant preserves purchasing power; real GDP rises about 3.8%
PM2B2-DEF-L-002.commonError: Chooses an index by familiarity rather than by the purpose of the comparison.
PM2B2-DEF-L-002.feedback: The grant and consumer-price factors are both 1.08, preserving purchasing power. GDP requires its own price factor: 1.08/1.04 - 1 ≈ 3.8%. Matching nominal rates do not imply matching real changes with different deflators.

PM2B2-DEF-LB-001.q: A country produces only $200 of export machinery and households consume only imported food. Machinery prices fall 4% while food prices rise 6%, with quantities fixed. Which pair is consistent?
options: CPI rises 6%; the GDP deflator falls 4%
CPI falls 4%; the GDP deflator rises 6%
Both indexes rise 6% because households pay that inflation
Both indexes fall 4% because domestic output determines every index
PM2B2-DEF-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “CPI falls 4%; the GDP deflator rises 6%” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
PM2B2-DEF-LB-001.feedback: Under the deliberately distinct baskets, CPI follows imported household food and the deflator follows domestic machinery, even though all machinery is exported.

PM2B2-DEF-MB-002.q: A domestic economy buys $220 of imported household fuel and produces machinery only for export. Fuel prices rise while machinery prices are unchanged. Which index selection and direction are appropriate, holding quantities fixed?
options: Both rise equally; household fuel belongs in both indexes at equal weight.
CPI is unchanged; the GDP deflator rises through the import-price component.
CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
Both are unchanged; imported consumption is excluded from either price index.
PM2B2-DEF-MB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Only the GDP deflator rises because imported fuel is subtracted through net exports” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
PM2B2-DEF-MB-002.feedback: CPI covers household consumption including imports. The GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output, including exports; unchanged domestic output prices need not reflect imported fuel inflation.

PM2B2-DEF-MB-003.q: A household benefit of $230 must track consumption costs, while an analyst must convert nominal domestic GDP into real output. Imported food becomes dearer and domestic investment equipment becomes cheaper. Which pairing and implication are supported?
options: CPI for both uses; consumer prices also measure domestic capital-goods prices.
CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
Deflator for both uses; domestic output prices measure imported household costs.
Deflator for benefits, CPI for GDP; imported food belongs to domestic output.
PM2B2-DEF-MB-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Use the GDP deflator for both; household consumption excludes imported food” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
PM2B2-DEF-MB-003.feedback: The purpose determines index choice. CPI tracks consumption costs; the deflator matches domestic final output. Imports and investment equipment enter these measures differently, so divergent movements are possible.

PM2B2-INDEX-L-003.q: A threshold is $40,000 at CPI 100. The contract adjusts next year using the previous year’s inflation. CPI rises to 110, then 121; by the second year the threshold has received only the first 10% adjustment. What is the shortfall from full current indexation?
options: $4,000; apply the second 10% only to the original threshold
$8,400; the threshold never received any adjustment
$4,400; the paid threshold is $44,000 instead of $48,400
$0; a one-year lag cannot alter purchasing power
PM2B2-INDEX-L-003.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
PM2B2-INDEX-L-003.feedback: Full current indexation requires 40,000 × 121/100 = 48,400. The lagged threshold is 40,000 × 1.10 = 44,000. The gap is 4,400; successive inflation rates apply to changing price levels.

PM2B2-INDEX-LB-001.q: A $180 benefit is adjusted by the previous year's 4% CPI rise. This year's cost of living rises 6%. Which result explains the limitation of this indexation rule?
options: The benefit rises 6% and real purchasing power is unchanged because any indexation is contemporaneous
The benefit rises 4% and real purchasing power rises 2% because inflation is subtracted in the opposite direction
The benefit rises 10% and real purchasing power rises 4% because both years are added
The benefit rises 4% but current real purchasing power falls about 1.9% because the adjustment lags
PM2B2-INDEX-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The benefit rises 6% and real purchasing power is unchanged because any indexation is contemporaneous” in this indexing and real values task.
PM2B2-INDEX-LB-001.feedback: The nominal factor is 1.04 and current prices rise by 1.06. Real value changes by 1.04/1.06−1 ≈ −1.89%; lagged indexation does not fully cover current inflation.

PM2B3-POL-FB-005.q: A government must choose between accelerating a useful research program and temporary purchases during a demand slump. Does the slump prove the research program has no value?
options: Yes; temporary government purchases permanently determine the economy's research productivity.
No; current stabilization and future capacity benefits are different margins in allocating scarce resources.
Yes; idle capacity makes every investment in future technology economically worthless.
No; research spending automatically eliminates the current output gap without a demand calculation.
PM2B3-POL-FB-005.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; idle capacity makes every investment in future technology economically worthless.
PM2B3-POL-FB-005.feedback: A slump creates a demand-management concern, but does not eliminate future benefits from research. Budget allocation should compare timing, expected benefits and opportunity costs; neither policy's value follows mechanically from the other's objective.

PM2B3-POL-FB-006.q: The graph suggests high marginal returns near A, but a country at A has unreliable contract enforcement that deters investment. Compare subsidizing machines alone with improving enforcement plus investment. Which inference respects the difference between potential and realized catch-up?
options: Enforcement plus investment addresses the constraint; potential returns alone do not ensure investment.
Machine subsidies alone ensure catch-up; investors' ability to retain returns is irrelevant.
Enforcement alone reaches B immediately; additional capital and production changes are unnecessary.
Neither policy can help at A; diminishing returns eliminate the incentive to invest.
PM2B3-POL-FB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Machine subsidies alone guarantee catch-up regardless of whether investors can retain returns” in this economic growth policy task.
PM2B3-POL-FB-006.feedback: The curve describes productive potential under maintained conditions. Weak enforcement can stop capital accumulation despite high physical returns. Addressing incentives complements capital deepening; it does not mechanically manufacture the required capital.

PM2B3-POL-H-001.q: GROWTH-01 shows that capital deepening can move an economy from A toward B, but the curve becomes flatter. Which policy implication is strongest?
options: Capital raises output, while sustained growth also needs broader productivity gains
Capital accumulation becomes completely useless as soon as the economy reaches point B on the graph
The graph implies that low-capital economies should stop investment before they approach point B
Long-run growth can rely on repeated physical-capital accumulation forever without complementary productivity improvements
PM2B3-POL-H-001.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
PM2B3-POL-H-001.feedback: Capital deepening raises output but faces diminishing returns; sustained growth also requires skills, technology, and sound institutions.

PM2B3-POL-LB-001.q: GROWTH-01 suggests catch-up through A→B. A planner proposes ever larger capital investment to maintain the initial growth rate indefinitely, with technology and all other productivity determinants fixed. Which alternative distinguishes a higher level from sustained growth?
options: Capital deepening preserves the initial marginal return indefinitely; research would only change nominal output
Diminishing returns imply no gain from A→B, so reducing capital is the growth strategy
Reaching B guarantees permanent growth even if all productive inputs and technology then stop changing
Capital deepening raises the level with diminishing gains; sustained productivity growth requires continuing improvements beyond capital alone
PM2B3-POL-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Capital deepening preserves the initial marginal return indefinitely; research would only change nominal output” in this economic growth policy task.
PM2B3-POL-LB-001.feedback: Diminishing returns make successive capital additions less productive. A finite catch-up level gain is not a permanent growth mechanism. Continuing technology/human-capital improvements can change the productive relation instead of relying only on movement along it.

PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.q: In GROWTH-01, A has output per worker about 28.53 and B about 36.37. If employment is identical, a report says doubling capital per worker from 20 to 40 doubles total output. Which correction uses both the graph and the fixed-employment condition?
options: Output rises 100%; doubling capital always doubles output even on a flattening curve
Output rises about 7.84%; subtracting productivity levels directly gives a percentage
Output falls about 21.6%; use the higher productivity as the initial value
Output rises about 27.5%, not 100%; fixed employment makes total output grow by that same percentage
PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Output rises 100%; doubling capital always doubles output even on a flattening curve” in this productivity measurement task.
PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.feedback: With identical employment, total-output growth equals output-per-worker growth: (36.37/28.53−1)×100≈27.5%. The flattening curve does not support proportional doubling.

PM2B3-PROD-FB-004.q: Use the displayed GROWTH-01 coordinates. Moving from A to B doubles capital per worker. Approximately how much does output per worker rise, and what is consistent with the curve’s shape?
options: 7.84%; the numerical output increase is already a percentage
27.5%; the same further capital increase would add less output
100%; doubling capital must double output
27.5%; each further equal capital increase must add more output
PM2B3-PROD-FB-004.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-FB-004.feedback: The graph gives output 28.53 at A and 36.37 at B. The increase is 7.84/28.53 × 100 ≈ 27.5%. The flattening curve shows diminishing marginal gains from equal additional capital, holding other inputs fixed.

PM2B3-PROD-H-001.q: GROWTH-01 becomes flatter as capital per worker rises. After moving from A to B, what should be expected from another equal increase in capital per worker, holding other factors constant?
options: A smaller additional gain in output per worker than the A-to-B gain
The same 7.84-unit gain by definition
A larger gain because the economy is richer
No further output gain is possible
PM2B3-PROD-H-001.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-H-001.feedback: The curve is flatter to the right, so an equal additional amount of capital produces a smaller marginal output gain than A-to-B.

PM2B3-PROD-L-001.q: In GROWTH-01, two otherwise similar economies begin at A and B. Each receives the same small addition to capital per worker. Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: Point A has the larger marginal output gain; convergence is not guaranteed
Point B must gain more because its current output per worker is already higher
Both economies must receive exactly the same output gain whenever capital increases by the same amount
Point A is guaranteed to overtake point B even if institutions and technology differ
PM2B3-PROD-L-001.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-L-001.feedback: The graph is steeper at A, so the same small capital addition yields a larger marginal output gain there; this alone does not guarantee convergence.

PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.q: A firm produces 2100 units at 10 units per labor hour. After training, productivity is 12 units per hour and required output rises to 2520. Which conclusion follows about labor hours and its limit?
options: Hours are zero; higher productivity replaces all labor
Hours remain 210; higher output exactly matches the proportional productivity gain
Hours rise to 252; output growth alone sets required hours
Hours fall to 175.0; apply the productivity gain but ignore higher required output
PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Hours are zero; higher productivity replaces all labor” in this productivity measurement task.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.feedback: Initial hours = 2100/10 = 210; new hours = 2520/12 = 210. Productivity gains do not necessarily reduce total hours when output demand changes too.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.roundingRule: Compute 1.25 ÷ 1.20 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.q: The GROWTH-01 curve shows productivity rising from A to B. Employment could rise or fall during that move. Which part of a claim that both productivity and total output must rise is established by the graph alone?
options: Productivity rises; total output depends on the accompanying employment change.
Productivity and total output rise; higher output per worker fixes both directions.
Only total output rises; the vertical axis measures aggregate rather than per-worker output.
Neither rises; diminishing returns make additional capital reduce output per worker.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both must rise; an increase in output per worker rules out falling total output” in this productivity measurement task.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.feedback: Output per worker rises from 28.53 to 36.37, but total output is productivity×workers. A workforce ratio below 28.53/36.37≈.7844 would more than offset that gain. Diminishing positive returns do not mean falling productivity.

PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.q: GROWTH-01 is steeper near A than B. Compare an equal small addition to capital per worker at each point, holding technology and other inputs per worker fixed. Which forecast is supported?
options: A larger productivity gain near A, but positive gains at both points
Equal productivity gains at both points because capital additions are equal
A larger gain near B because its initial productivity is higher
A gain near A and a loss near B because diminishing returns turn output negative
PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Equal productivity gains at both points because capital additions are equal” in this sources of productivity task.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.feedback: The slope measures the marginal productivity effect of capital deepening. The curve is positive but flatter near B: the marginal gain is smaller, not negative.

PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.q: In GROWTH-01, capital deepening takes the economy A→B on one curve. A later observation lies above that curve at the same capital per worker as B. Which explanation distinguishes the two changes?
options: Both show falling marginal productivity means falling total productivity
A→B is capital deepening; the later gain requires another productive factor or technology to improve
Both are movements along the same curve caused only by more capital per worker
A→B is a technology shift; the later gain is diminishing returns to unchanged capital
PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both show falling marginal productivity means falling total productivity” in this sources of productivity task.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.feedback: Moving along the curve changes capital with the other determinants held fixed. Higher output at the same capital requires a changed productive condition, such as technology or human capital.

PM2B4-LMI-BR-001.q: A new job-matching service reduces the average time workers spend between jobs. What family-level implication follows?
options: Lower frictional unemployment can reduce the natural rate
Lower frictional unemployment must raise cyclical unemployment
The natural rate is fixed and cannot respond to matching
Only the measured CPI can change from better matching
PM2B4-LMI-BR-001.commonError: Failing to connect institutions that change search efficiency with the frictional component of the natural rate.
PM2B4-LMI-BR-001.feedback: Faster matching reduces frictional unemployment; because frictional unemployment is part of the natural rate, the natural rate can fall.

PM2B4-LMI-EB-003.q: A benefit reform gives 270 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
options: Longer search raises frictional costs; better retention adds benefits; welfare needs both.
Longer search raises frictional costs; better retention adds nothing; welfare necessarily falls.
Better retention adds benefits; longer search adds no cost; welfare necessarily rises.
Longer search is cyclical; better retention is structural; frictional costs remain unchanged.
PM2B4-LMI-EB-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Longer search proves the reform reduced job-match quality despite better observed retention” in this labor market institutions task.
PM2B4-LMI-EB-003.feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.

PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.q: An economy has frictional unemployment 2%, structural 3% and actual 6%. If a demand recovery removes the cyclical component without changing matching or skills, which rate remains and why?
options: 5%; frictional and structural remain after the cyclical point disappears.
0%; removing cyclical unemployment also removes frictional and structural components.
3%; frictional unemployment disappears with the cyclical component during recovery.
6%; changes in demand leave all three unemployment components unchanged.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “0%; eliminating cyclical unemployment eliminates every component” in this natural rate of unemployment task.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.feedback: Natural unemployment=2+3=5; the initial cyclical component is 6−5=1. Recovery alone does not remove search and structural mismatch.

PM2C2-FISH-EB-001.q: A $200 fixed-rate loan has nominal interest 7% when expected inflation is 3%. Actual inflation later turns out to be 6%. Which pair separates the rate-setting prediction from the realized outcome?
options: The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed
Both expected and realized real returns are 4% because the lender chose a fixed nominal rate
The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate
The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the signed nominal rate
PM2C2-FISH-EB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed” in this fisher effect task.
PM2C2-FISH-EB-001.feedback: Fisher rate setting uses expected inflation at agreement; ex post purchasing power uses actual inflation. Thus 7−3=4% expected and 7−6=1% realized; the nominal contract remains 7%.

PM2C2-FISH-FB-006.q: A $280 fixed-rate loan has nominal interest 7% when expected inflation is 3%. Actual inflation later turns out to be 6%. Which pair separates the rate-setting prediction from the realized outcome?
options: The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate
The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the signed nominal rate
The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed
Both expected and realized real returns are 4% because the lender chose a fixed nominal rate
PM2C2-FISH-FB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate” in this fisher effect task.
PM2C2-FISH-FB-006.feedback: Fisher rate setting uses expected inflation at agreement; ex post purchasing power uses actual inflation. Thus 7−3=4% expected and 7−6=1% realized; the nominal contract remains 7%.

PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.q: A household owes a fixed nominal $300. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.

PM2C3-LPMM-BR-001.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, raising the equilibrium interest rate. What is the next step if the student is bridging from the money market to monetary-policy transmission?
options: Higher borrowing costs reduce interest-sensitive investment and put downward pressure on aggregate demand.
Higher borrowing costs raise investment because firms earn more interest.
The higher interest rate directly increases government purchases.
Aggregate demand is unaffected because interest rates matter only inside the money-market graph.
PM2C3-LPMM-BR-001.commonError: Stops after finding the new money-market interest rate and does not carry the result into spending and aggregate demand.
PM2C3-LPMM-BR-001.feedback: After solving the money market, use the interest-rate change to infer the direction of investment and other rate-sensitive spending, then the aggregate-demand shift.

PM2C3-LPMM-L-001.q: Refer to the money-market graph. Starting at point e (MS1 with MD1), both money demand and money supply shift right to MD2 and MS2. The new equilibrium is point d. What does the change from r2 to r3 imply?
options: The rightward money-demand shift exerts more upward pressure on the interest rate than the rightward money-supply shift offsets.
The money-supply shift must have dominated because any increase in money supply mechanically raises interest rates more than a simultaneous money-demand shift can affect them.
Both rightward shifts necessarily leave the interest rate unchanged.
The new equilibrium shows that money demand fell relative to money supply.
PM2C3-LPMM-L-001.commonError: Assumes the direction of one curve shift determines the interest rate even when both money demand and money supply move.
PM2C3-LPMM-L-001.feedback: When money demand and money supply both shift, compare the new equilibrium with the old one; the interest-rate direction depends on their relative effects.

PM2C3-LPMM-L-006.q: Refer to the money-market graph. The economy begins at e with MD1 and MS1. Money demand shifts to MD2, and the central bank also expands money supply to MS2. Is the increase in money supply large enough to keep the interest rate at r2?
options: Yes. Any rightward money-supply shift exactly offsets any rightward money-demand shift.
Yes. Point d lies on MS2, so the interest rate must still equal r2.
No. The central bank would need to reduce money supply to keep the interest rate from rising.
No. The new equilibrium d is at r3, so the central bank would need a larger rightward money-supply shift to hold the rate at r2.
PM2C3-LPMM-L-006.commonError: Uses a contractionary money-supply response to offset a rightward money-demand shift.
PM2C3-LPMM-L-006.feedback: If money demand shifts right and the central bank wants to prevent the interest rate from rising, it must increase money supply enough to accommodate the higher demand.
PM2C3-LPMM-L-006.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.

PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.q: With MD2 and MS2, point b is above equilibrium d. Compare the initial asset-market adjustment with a counterfactual central-bank sale that reduces supply to MS1 before rates adjust. Which two conclusions follow?
options: Initially excess money prompts bond sales and higher rates; the sale makes g the new equilibrium at a lower rate
Initially a money shortage prompts bond sales and higher rates; the sale makes e the new equilibrium on MD1
Initially a money shortage prompts bond purchases and lower rates; the sale leaves d unchanged
Initially excess money prompts bond purchases and lower rates; the sale makes a the new equilibrium at the original higher rate
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Initially excess money prompts bond sales and higher rates; the sale makes g the new equilibrium at a lower rate” in this liquidity preference and money market task.
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.feedback: At b under MS2/MD2, money supplied exceeds desired balances, inducing bond purchases and downward rate pressure toward d. Reducing supply to MS1 changes the relevant equilibrium to a on MD2 at r4. The policy changes the equilibrium, rather than reversing the asset adjustment at the original curves.

Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

PM2C3-LPMM-LB-002.q: Refer to the money-market graph. The economy moves from e to d because both money demand and money supply shift right. Which conclusion is supported by the final interest rate?
options: The supply shift dominates, because every increase in money supply raises the interest rate.
The two shifts exactly offset, because both curves move right.
Money demand must have shifted left, because the equilibrium quantity of money rises.
The demand shift dominates the supply shift’s interest-rate effect, because the equilibrium rate rises from r2 to r3.
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-002.commonError: Assumes the direction of one curve shift determines the interest rate even when both money demand and money supply move.
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-002.feedback: When money demand and money supply both shift, compare the new equilibrium with the old one; the interest-rate direction depends on their relative effects.

PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.q: At AD1-AS1 the graph places output at Y3 below potential Y1. Demand stays fixed. Which wage adjustment and output movement would close this gap?
options: Rising expected wages/costs shift AS2 toward AS1 and raise output toward Y1
Falling expected wages/costs shift AD1 toward AD2 and lower output toward Y3
Rising expected wages/costs shift LRAS toward Y3 and increase productive capacity
Falling expected wages/costs shift AS1 toward AS2 and raise output toward Y1
PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Rising expected wages/costs shift AS2 toward AS1 and raise output toward Y1” in this ad as equilibrium and output gaps task.
PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.feedback: A recessionary gap puts downward pressure on expected wages/costs. With demand fixed, supply shifts right toward AS2, returning output toward Y1.

PM2D1-LRADJ-L-001.q: Refer to the graph. A demand increase has moved the economy to the intersection of AD2 and AS2 at Y2 and P2. If no policy reverses AD2 and long-run adjustment is completed, which comparison between the short-run and long-run effects is supported by the graph?
options: The temporary output gain disappears as output returns to Y1, while the price level rises further toward P3.
Output remains at Y2 because long-run adjustment changes only the price level, which falls all the way back toward P1.
Output falls to Y3 as SRAS shifts left past AS1, while the price level stays fixed at the short-run level P2.
Both real output and the price level return to their original Y1 and P1 values once wage contracts and expectations adjust.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-001.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-001.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.q: At AD1-AS1/Y3, wages start falling. Before adjustment ends, demand falls further left of AD1. Which conclusion can still be drawn without the sizes of the two shifts?
options: Wages support recovery; further demand loss makes the final output change uncertain.
Wages ensure recovery to Y1; the supply shift dominates the added demand loss.
Demand ensures a further output fall; the demand shift dominates falling wages.
Both changes lower potential output; combined AD and SRAS shifts move LRAS left.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Output must reach Y1 immediately because any rightward supply shift dominates demand” in this long run macroeconomic self adjustment task.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.feedback: Rightward AS adjustment raises output relative to unchanged demand, while a new demand contraction lowers it. Relative magnitudes determine the net output path; LRAS need not move.

PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.q: At AD1-AS1/Y3, nominal wages are fixed by contracts for one year. Officials predict immediate self-correction to Y1 solely through lower wages. Which part of that prediction conflicts with the stated constraint?
options: Neither is appropriate because returning to Y1 requires LRAS to move left
The direction is appropriate but the claimed timing is not: wage-based AS adjustment must wait for contracts
The timing is appropriate but the direction is not: lower wages shift AS left
Both are appropriate because contracts cannot affect short-run supply adjustment
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Neither is appropriate because returning to Y1 requires LRAS to move left” in this long run macroeconomic self adjustment task.
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.feedback: Lower wages would shift AS1 toward AS2, but fixed contracts prevent that wage mechanism from completing immediately. Distinguish eventual direction from adjustment speed.

PM2E-CH-FINAL-002.q: An oil-price shock lowers real output while raising inflation and unemployment. Why is this a harder stabilization problem than an ordinary demand-side recession?
options: Supporting output can worsen inflation, while restraining inflation can deepen the output and unemployment loss.
Supporting output can reduce unemployment, but because inflation originated from aggregate demand, inflation will necessarily fall as output recovers.
Restraining aggregate demand can reduce inflation, but it may also lower output further before the supply-side problem is resolved.
Because inflation and unemployment rise together, policymakers can stabilize both by returning aggregate demand to its original level.
PM2E-CH-FINAL-002.commonError: Treating a supply shock as if it were a conventional demand recession with one obvious policy direction.
PM2E-CH-FINAL-002.feedback: An adverse supply shock creates a stabilization tradeoff because expansionary demand policy can support output and employment but worsen inflation, while contractionary demand policy can reduce inflation pressure but further weaken output and employment.

PMOE-FX-B3-003.q: In FX-03, supply expands and the foreign-units-per-domestic-unit rate falls from 1 to 0.8 while quantity rises 100→150. An importer faces an unchanged foreign price. Which rate, quantity and home-currency import-cost comparison is correct?
options: Domestic currency appreciates 25%, quantity rises 50%, and the home import cost falls 20%
Domestic currency depreciates 20%, quantity rises 33.3%, and the home import cost falls 25%
Domestic currency depreciates 20%, traded quantity rises 50%, and the home cost of the import rises 25%
Domestic currency depreciates 20%, quantity rises 50%, and the home import cost rises 20%
PMOE-FX-B3-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Domestic currency appreciates 25%, quantity rises 50%, and the home import cost falls 20%” in this foreign exchange market task.
PMOE-FX-B3-003.feedback: Rate change=.8/1−1=−20%; quantity change=150/100−1=50%. Home currency per foreign unit rises from 1 to 1/.8=1.25, increasing a fixed foreign-price import cost 25%. Reciprocal percentage changes are not symmetric.
PMOE-FX-B3-003.imageAlt: Upward-sloping dollar supply shifts right from S0 to S1 along demand D0.

Demand D0 is unchanged while supply shifts right from solid S0 to dashed S1. Equilibrium moves from A at quantity 100 and rate 1.0 to B at quantity 150 and rate 0.8.
PMOE-FX-B3-003.foreignExchangeScenario: Increase in supply of U.S. dollars

PMOE-FX-EL-002.q: Refer to the numbered graph with upward-sloping dollar supply and e in foreign currency per dollar. A to B shows unchanged e after both curves shift right. A report attributes this to no change in demand. Which evidence rejects that claim, and can the final rate identify which shift occurred first?
options: S1 differs from S0, proving demand did not change; the final rate identifies supply first
Quantity rises, proving e must have risen; the final rate identifies demand first
The unchanged rate proves the curves did not move; their order is irrelevant
D1 differs from D0 and quantity rises; the final rate does not identify shift order
PMOE-FX-EL-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “S1 differs from S0, proving demand did not change; the final rate identifies supply first” in this foreign exchange market task.
PMOE-FX-EL-002.feedback: The image visibly shows both D and S shifts and a larger quantity. Their rate effects offset in the final equilibrium, but that endpoint does not reveal whether demand or supply shifted first.
PMOE-FX-EL-002.imageAlt: Dollar demand and upward-sloping supply both shift right, from D0 and S0 to D1 and S1.
PMOE-FX-EL-002.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand and supply both shift right. D1 crosses S0 at approximately quantity 150 and rate 1.2; D0 crosses S1 at approximately quantity 150 and rate 0.8. These two crossings have no point labels or dashed coordinate guides.
PMOE-FX-EL-002.foreignExchangeScenario: Simultaneous increases in demand and supply

PMOE-FX-L-002.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose foreign demand caused the move from D0 to D1. With domestic and foreign price levels fixed, how does the new rate tend to affect net exports?
options: The appreciation restrains NX, creating movement along the new demand relationship
The appreciation reinforces exports while leaving imports unchanged
The higher foreign-currency price of a dollar makes domestic exports cheaper
The rate change shifts currency supply right by the same amount
PMOE-FX-L-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The appreciation reinforces exports while leaving imports unchanged” in this foreign exchange market task.
PMOE-FX-L-002.feedback: With price levels fixed, the nominal appreciation is also a real appreciation. Domestic goods become relatively expensive, offsetting part of the initial export-demand increase.
PMOE-FX-L-002.imageAlt: Dollar demand shifts right from D0 to D1 while upward-sloping supply S0 remains fixed.
PMOE-FX-L-002.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand shifts right from solid D0 to dashed D1 along unchanged upward-sloping S0. Equilibrium moves from A at quantity 100 and rate 1.0 to B at quantity 150 and rate 1.2.
PMOE-FX-L-002.foreignExchangeScenario: Increase in demand for U.S. dollars

PMOE-FX-L-003.q: Refer to the graph showing S0 shifting right to S1 along D0. Prices are fixed. One explanation is lower domestic real returns; another is higher domestic political risk. What do the displayed rate and quantity changes identify, and what additional evidence distinguishes these explanations?
options: Lower domestic real returns uniquely; the supply shift rules out political risk
Higher political risk uniquely; depreciation rules out a return change
A rise in dollar demand; the same image cannot be produced by a supply shock
A larger dollar supply and real depreciation; independent return or risk evidence is needed to identify the cause
PMOE-FX-L-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Lower domestic real returns uniquely; the supply shift rules out political risk” in this foreign exchange market task.
PMOE-FX-L-003.feedback: The new intersection is rightward and lower, so with fixed prices the dollar depreciates in nominal and real terms. Both lower domestic returns and greater domestic risk can raise supply through asset purchases; the graph alone does not choose the source.
PMOE-FX-L-003.imageAlt: Upward-sloping dollar supply shifts right from S0 to S1 along demand D0.
PMOE-FX-L-003.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand D0 is unchanged while supply shifts right from solid S0 to dashed S1. Equilibrium moves from A at quantity 100 and rate 1.0 to B at quantity 150 and rate 0.8.
PMOE-FX-L-003.foreignExchangeScenario: Increase in supply of U.S. dollars

PMOE-FX-LB-001.q: Refer to the conceptual graph with upward-sloping supply. Foreign export demand shifts D0 to D1 and residents’ foreign-asset purchases shift S0 to S1. Separately, foreign purchases of domestic assets are known to be unchanged. Which conclusion distinguishes graph evidence from asset accounting?
options: The unchanged rate alone proves unchanged NCO even though residents buy more foreign assets
The gross dollar quantity alone equals NCO in every upward-sloping currency market
The displayed quantity rises and the rate rises; the identity permits NX to fall despite higher NCO
The displayed dollar quantity rises and the rate is unchanged; the separate net-asset evidence establishes higher NCO and therefore NX
PMOE-FX-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The unchanged rate alone proves unchanged NCO even though residents buy more foreign assets” in this foreign exchange market task.
PMOE-FX-LB-001.feedback: The graph provides a rightward final intersection at the same vertical level. NCO rises because resident foreign purchases rise with the inward asset flow fixed, not because gross currency turnover is itself NCO. In consistent accounts, NX matches that higher NCO.
PMOE-FX-LB-001.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market showing demand and upward-sloping supply both shifting right.
PMOE-FX-LB-001.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand shifts right from D0 to D1 and supply shifts right from S0 to S1. The displayed shifts raise equilibrium quantity while leaving the exchange rate at the same vertical position. No numerical ticks are shown.
PMOE-FX-LB-001.foreignExchangeScenario: Conceptual simultaneous increases in demand and supply

PMOE-FX-LB-003.q: Refer to the numbered graph. Compare demand-first and supply-first adjustment, assuming each market clears before the second shift and final curves are identical. Which statement distinguishes the paths from the endpoint?
options: Both paths temporarily raise the rate because final quantity is larger
Demand first temporarily raises the rate and supply first temporarily lowers it; both end at B
Demand first ends at a permanently higher rate than supply first
Both paths have a constant rate because A and B have the same rate
PMOE-FX-LB-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both paths temporarily raise the rate because final quantity is larger” in this foreign exchange market task.
PMOE-FX-LB-003.feedback: D1 with S0 crosses above A; D0 with S1 crosses below A. Once both changes occur, each path ends at the same unique D1-S1 intersection B. An unchanged endpoint does not imply an unchanged intermediate rate.
PMOE-FX-LB-003.imageAlt: Dollar demand and upward-sloping supply both shift right, from D0 and S0 to D1 and S1.
PMOE-FX-LB-003.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand and supply both shift right. Original equilibrium A is quantity 100 and rate 1.0; final equilibrium B is quantity 200 and rate 1.0. Solid curves are D0 and S0; dashed curves are D1 and S1. D1 crosses S0 at approximately quantity 150 and rate 1.2; D0 crosses S1 at approximately quantity 150 and rate 0.8. These two crossings have no point labels or dashed coordinate guides.
PMOE-FX-LB-003.foreignExchangeScenario: Simultaneous increases in demand and supply

PMOE-FX-M-006.q: Refer to the conceptual graph. Where is the market equilibrium?
options: At the vertical-axis intercept of D0
At every point on S0
At the horizontal-axis intercept of D0
At the intersection of D0 and S0
PMOE-FX-M-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “At the vertical-axis intercept of D0” in this foreign exchange market task.
PMOE-FX-M-006.feedback: Market equilibrium occurs where the quantity of dollars demanded equals the quantity supplied.
PMOE-FX-M-006.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market with downward-sloping demand D0 and upward-sloping supply S0.
PMOE-FX-M-006.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar. The horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 intersects upward-sloping S0. No numerical ticks or point labels are shown.

PMOE-NER-LB-002.q: A British product's pound price rises 6 percent, the pound depreciates 8 percent against the dollar, and U.S. sales volume rises 5 percent. Approximately what happens to the exporter's dollar revenue?
options: It falls about 2.5 percent
It rises about 11 percent
It falls about 7.4 percent
It rises about 2.4 percent
PMOE-NER-LB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It falls about 2.5 percent” in this nominal exchange rates task.
PMOE-NER-LB-002.feedback: Dollar revenue changes by 1.06×0.92×1.05 − 1 ≈ 0.024, so it rises about 2.4 percent.

PMOE-NER-LB-003.q: The yen first appreciates 10 percent and then depreciates 10 percent, each measured in U.S. dollars per yen from the preceding value. A yen-denominated asset meanwhile gains 4 percent. What is its cumulative dollar return, and what final currency rise alone would restore the initial dollars-per-yen quote?
options: A 4 percent asset return; no further currency change
A 3 percent asset return; exactly a 1 percent currency rise
A 2.96 percent asset return; about a 1.01 percent currency rise
A 5.04 percent asset return; about a 1.01 percent currency decline
PMOE-NER-LB-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A 4 percent asset return; no further currency change” in this nominal exchange rates task.
PMOE-NER-LB-003.feedback: The quote factor is 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99. The dollar asset factor is 0.99 × 1.04 = 1.0296. Restoring the currency quote requires 1/0.99 − 1 ≈ 1.01 percent, separate from the asset return.

PMOE-POL-B2-001.q: Refer to the conceptual graph. A deficit raises domestic rates and lowers NCO. Which displayed change represents the next link?
options: Vertical dollar supply shifts left from S0 to S1
Dollar demand shifts right from D0 to D1
Vertical dollar supply shifts right from S1 to S0
Dollar demand becomes vertical at S0
PMOE-POL-B2-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Dollar demand shifts right from D0 to D1” in this open economy policy transmission task.
PMOE-POL-B2-001.feedback: Lower NCO means fewer dollars are exchanged for foreign assets, represented by the leftward shift in NCO-determined supply.
PMOE-POL-B2-001.imageAlt: Conceptual Mankiw-model dollar market with vertical supply shifting left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1.
PMOE-POL-B2-001.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 equals NX0. Vertical supply shifts left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1, so the new intersection is above and left of the original intersection. No numerical ticks or point labels are shown.
PMOE-POL-B2-001.foreignExchangeScenario: Conceptual decrease in NCO-determined supply of U.S. dollars

PMOE-POL-EL-002.q: In a short-run comparison before full trade and output adjustment, monetary easing lowers domestic real rates while a foreign recession cuts export demand. Prices are fixed, and NCO is not held fixed across the two shocks. Can the net AD change be signed without response magnitudes?
options: AD falls because foreign income changes exports while monetary policy changes only investment
AD is unchanged because depreciation offsets the export-demand shift one for one
Ambiguous without the relative strengths of higher NX from depreciation and lower export demand
AD rises because the monetary channel determines the exchange rate before exports respond
PMOE-POL-EL-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD falls because foreign income changes exports while monetary policy changes only investment” in this open economy policy transmission task.
PMOE-POL-EL-002.feedback: Easing supports domestic investment and, through depreciation, NX. Foreign recession reduces demand for exports. Their short-run AD contributions compete. The fixed-NCO long-run trade-offset result cannot be imposed on this adjustment comparison.

PMOE-POL-L-002.q: In the open-economy loanable-funds model, saving is unchanged and capital flight raises desired NCO $150 billion at the original real interest rate. Final domestic investment falls $110 billion. Reconstruct the rate-induced NCO feedback and FX outcome with NX demand and price levels fixed.
options: Feedback raises NCO $40 billion; final NCO rises $190 billion and the currency depreciates
Feedback lowers NCO $110 billion; final NCO rises $40 billion and the currency appreciates
Feedback exactly cancels the shock; NCO and the exchange rate are unchanged
Feedback lowers NCO $40 billion; final NCO rises $110 billion and the currency depreciates
PMOE-POL-L-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Feedback raises NCO $40 billion; final NCO rises $190 billion and the currency depreciates” in this open economy policy transmission task.
PMOE-POL-L-002.feedback: With ΔS=0 and ΔI=−110, ΔNCO=110. Relative to the initial +150 schedule shift, rate feedback is −40. Final vertical FX supply shifts right by 110, lowering the foreign-currency-per-domestic-currency rate and raising NX.

PMOE-POL-M-003.q: Refer to the graph. What happens to the U.S. dollar when NCO-determined supply shifts left from S0 to S1?
options: It appreciates while the dollar quantity rises from 50 to 100
It appreciates from 1.0 to 1.5 foreign-currency units per dollar
It depreciates from 1.5 to 1.0 foreign-currency units per dollar
It remains fixed because NX equals NCO
PMOE-POL-M-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It appreciates while the dollar quantity rises from 50 to 100” in this open economy policy transmission task.
PMOE-POL-M-003.feedback: The leftward supply shift moves equilibrium from A to B, raising the foreign-currency price of a dollar while reducing quantity from 100 to 50.
PMOE-POL-M-003.imageAlt: Mankiw-model dollar market with vertical supply shifting left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1 along D0 equals NX0.
PMOE-POL-M-003.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 equals NX0. Vertical supply shifts left from S0 equals NCO0 at quantity 100 to S1 equals NCO1 at quantity 50. Equilibrium moves from A at rate 1.0 to B at rate 1.5.
PMOE-POL-M-003.foreignExchangeScenario: Decrease in NCO-determined supply of U.S. dollars

PMOE-RER-L-001.q: The nominal rate rises from 1.20 to 1.26 foreign units per domestic unit, domestic prices rise 4 percent, and foreign prices rise 10 percent. Approximately what happens to the real exchange rate?
options: It depreciates about 5 percent
It appreciates about 1 percent
It depreciates about 1 percent
It appreciates about 11 percent
PMOE-RER-L-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It depreciates about 5 percent” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
PMOE-RER-L-001.feedback: The exact factor is 1.05×1.04/1.10 ≈ 0.993, a real depreciation of about 0.7 percent.

PMOE-RER-LB-002.q: Let e be foreign currency per domestic currency and ε = eP/P*. A domestic basket rises from 250 to 270 domestic currency units, its foreign counterpart rises from 400 to 408 foreign currency units, and e falls from 1.60 to 1.50. What is the final real rate compared with the initial rate?
options: It rises from 1.00 to about 1.08
It falls from 1.60 to 1.50
It remains exactly 1.00
It falls from 1.00 to about 0.993
PMOE-RER-LB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It rises from 1.00 to about 1.08” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.

PMOE-TX-B3-001.q: Private saving rises $40 billion, public saving falls $15 billion, and domestic investment rises $10 billion. A trade ledger reports exports up $20 billion and imports up $10 billion. Under S−I=NX, with no statistical discrepancy and all saving/investment figures held fixed, which correction reconciles the ledgers?
options: NX must rise $35 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must fall $15 billion
NX must fall $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $35 billion
NX must rise $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $5 billion
NX must rise $10 billion; revise saving down $5 billion despite the instruction to hold it fixed
PMOE-TX-B3-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “NX must rise $35 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must fall $15 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
PMOE-TX-B3-001.feedback: National saving rises 40−15=25; subtract investment growth 10 to obtain NX growth 15. Since ΔNX=ΔX−ΔM, 15=20−ΔM implies imports rise 5. The original trade ledger's 10-point NX increase fails the identity under the stated constraints.
